analysis.one_liner: Limits lawsuits over federal forest logging by cutting attorney fees, capping injunctions, and routing disputes into arbitration.
analysis.headline: The bill never received a hearing, vote, or cosponsor in two years and died when the 118th Congress ended on January 3, 2025.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would make it much harder to challenge logging projects on national forests and other federal timber lands in court. It would stop courts from awarding attorney fees to people who sue over these projects, cap court orders halting a project at 60 days, require judges to weigh the ecosystem effects of logging against the effects of not logging, and set up a binding arbitration pilot program that replaces judicial review for some disputes. The bill died in committee without any hearing or vote.
analysis.who_benefits: Timber companies and logging contractors on federal land, because court injunctions that stop or delay harvests would be shorter and harder to get, attorney-fee awards to challengers would end, and some disputes would move to arbitration where the selection criteria explicitly include timber production. Federal land agencies also gain, because they get more discretion to send objections to a binding process that is largely shielded from court review.

how_it_helps.text: A court considering an injunction against a logging project would have to balance the ecosystem effects of doing the project against not doing it, a framing that makes halting timber work harder to justify.
Any preliminary injunction or stay halting a forest management project could last no more than 60 days, though a court could renew it with updated information.

Plaintiffs who challenge these projects could no longer recover attorney fees or expenses from the Treasury's Claims and Judgment Fund, removing the fee-shifting that lets small groups afford to sue the government.

Agriculture and Interior would set up arbitration pilot programs that replace judicial review for designated disputes, capped at 10 arbitrations per region per year, with binding decisions that are not subject to judicial review.
Arbitrators choosing between proposals must weigh timber production alongside forest health, wildfire, insects, and property loss.

analysis.who_pays: Citizens and public-interest groups that want to challenge federal logging projects lose their fee awards, face sharply limited injunctions, and for some disputes would be shunted into a binding arbitration process the agency itself controls. Communities that wanted a court to block a specific project before it cut would have at most a 60-day window.

drawbacks.text: Ending attorney-fee awards removes the main way small nonprofits and individual citizens can afford to litigate against the federal government, effectively pricing most citizens out of these challenges.
A 60-day cap on preliminary injunctions could let logging proceed before a court finishes deciding whether the project is lawful.
Arbitration decisions would be binding and largely exempt from judicial review, and the agency's choice of which disputes get shunted into arbitration could not be challenged in court either.

Supporters argue that litigation routinely delays fuel-reduction work and raises wildfire risk to nearby communities; an honest objection is that the bill attacks court access broadly rather than speeding legitimate review of fire-reduction projects.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: Speeding up forest treatment to reduce wildfire risk is a real public concern, but the bill's tools — a fee ban that prices out most challengers, a short fuse on injunctions, and binding arbitration shielded from review — remove public checks on logging decisions more than they improve review speed. The timber production criteria written into the arbitration process make clear which direction the bill tilts.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to three House committees and then to two subcommittees, and nothing else ever happened to it before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Matt Rosendale introduced the bill on January 30, 2023, with no cosponsors.
It was referred to the Natural Resources, Agriculture, and Judiciary Committees on the day it was introduced.
In late February 2023 it was referred to the Federal Lands and Forestry subcommittees, the last action ever taken on it.
No hearing, markup, or vote ever occurred, and the bill expired when the 118th Congress ended on January 3, 2025.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Citizens and conservation groups keep their current ability to challenge federal logging projects in court, including fee awards that make such suits affordable; timber interests gained nothing beyond the status quo they already had.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Citizens who sue over federal logging

for.name: Rep. Matthew Rosendale Sr.
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and was its sole sponsor; no other member signed on.

against.name: House Natural Resources Committee
against.role: Primary committee of referral; never scheduled a hearing or markup
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on January 30, 2023, sent it to the Federal Lands Subcommittee on February 21, and took no further action.

against.name: House Agriculture and Judiciary Committees
against.role: Additional committees of referral; never acted on the bill
against.what_they_did: Received referrals on the day of introduction and never considered the bill; Agriculture sent it to the Forestry Subcommittee on February 23, 2023, with nothing after.

sides.party_line_note: No votes were ever taken; the bill had a single Republican sponsor and zero cosponsors from either party, so it never developed a measurable partisan shape.

industries.industry: Timber and logging companies on federal land
industries.note: Shorter injunctions, no fee awards to challengers, and arbitration criteria that explicitly count timber production would all make it easier to log lands designated for timber production. The industry's gain comes directly at the cost of the public's ability to challenge those harvests in court.

The bill eliminates the fee-shifting that makes it financially possible for small nonprofits to sue the government, and channels some disputes into binding arbitration the agency controls. Their loss in court access is the public's loss too.

Faster resolution of challenges could speed fire-risk reduction projects that protect nearby communities. But the bill speeds this by limiting review of all qualified projects, including commercial timber harvests, not just fire work.
